summary: Records the MPLS Working Group's consensus to focus on RSVP-TE, from RFC 3209, as the signaling protocol for traffic engineering, and not to start new work on constraint-based LDP from RFC 3212.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3468 records the Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Working Group's choice to focus on one method for setting up traffic-engineered paths. It also explains why the group stopped new work on the competing method without changing the existing RFCs' status.

questions: why did the mpls working group choose rsvp-te
subtitle: The MPLS Working Group's decision to focus new traffic-engineering work on RSVP-TE.

tldr.problem: The MPLS Working Group had two standards-track approaches for signaling traffic-engineered label-switched paths, which led to parallel work and difficulty choosing a focus.
tldr.mechanism: The group agreed to focus on RSVP-TE and undertake no new CR-LDP work, while keeping RFC 3212 and related RFCs at their existing Proposed Standard status.
tldr.outcome: The IESG accepted the recommendations. The RFC records a working-group decision and process, not a protocol specification or a change in CR-LDP's status.

today: RFC 3468 is Informational and updates RFC 3212, RFC 3472, RFC 3475, and RFC 3476, according to the unit metadata. It records the decision to focus new MPLS traffic-engineering signaling work on RSVP-TE and does not obsolete those documents.

sections.title: What RFC 3468 Records
sections.content:
RFC 3468 documents consensus in the MPLS Working Group to continue developing RSVP-TE, defined in RFC 3209, for MPLS traffic-engineering signaling. It also records agreement to take on no new work related to CR-LDP, defined in RFC 3212.

The RFC is not a protocol specification. Its first five sections describe the background and consensus process; section 6 recommends actions to the IESG, which the abstract says were accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC records which method the Multiprotocol Label Switching group would continue developing to set up network paths. It does not define how either method works.

sections.title: Why the Group Reconsidered Its Focus
sections.content:
Two approaches had developed: extending RSVP for MPLS tunnels and extending LDP for constraint-based paths. The group had not reached consensus on one approach, and both had progressed to Proposed Standard.

A 2002 survey received responses from 22 implementers: 21 reported GMPLS signaling based on RFC 3209 and 3 reported signaling based on RFC 3212. This survey prompted discussion about maintaining two approaches and the duplicate work they created.
sections.plainLanguage: The group had two approaches for setting up traffic-engineered paths and had not agreed which to focus on. More survey respondents reported implementing the RSVP-based approach.

sections.title: Why CR-LDP Was Not Demoted
sections.content:
An early proposal would have moved CR-LDP to Informational status. Participants raised concerns that other standards organizations referenced RFC 3212 and that the IETF process did not describe how to move a standards-track document to a non-standards-track status. The RFC says these concerns made that proposal unworkable.

The revised proposal kept the document status unchanged but ended new working-group work on CR-LDP. The group also agreed to complete several existing drafts as appropriate, discourage further individual CR-LDP work without prohibiting it, and notify relevant standards organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: The group decided not to change the status of the existing documents because other organizations referenced them and the process was unclear. Instead, it stopped starting new group work on that approach.

sections.title: The Recommendation to the IESG
sections.content:
The working-group consensus was to focus on RSVP-TE, undertake no new CR-LDP work, and not promote RFC 3212 or related RFCs beyond Proposed Standard. Existing related working-group drafts could continue through the process. Individual contributions remained possible but were discouraged.

The RFC asked the IESG to confirm the focus, adopt policies against advancing CR-LDP work, review how the IETF manages standards-track status changes, and publish this decision as an Informational RFC. It states that the document adds no security or IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The group chose the RSVP-based method as its focus for new work on traffic-engineered paths. The other method's documents kept their status, but the group would not take on new work to advance them.
